title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch two BFS waves launch at once—one from the start, one from the goal—until they meet. This Bidirectional BFS on a city grid cuts the explored search space and speeds up shortest-path routing.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

On a street grid, standard BFS expands outward layer-by-layer from the start. Bidirectional BFS instead runs BFS from BOTH ends at the same time, alternating expansions until the frontiers intersect.

✅ Key idea (the “meeting”):
- Maintain two queues: one for Start→…, one for Goal→…
- Keep visited sets for each direction
- When a node appears in BOTH visited sets, you found a shortest path

🧠 Why it’s faster:
If the branching factor is b and the shortest path length is d, regular BFS explores ~b^d nodes. Bidirectional BFS targets ~2·b^(d/2), which is dramatically smaller—especially when d is large.

📌 Takeaway:
When you need the shortest path and the graph is unweighted, “bidirectional” is one of the cleanest graph optimization wins you can implement.

Debate question: Would you use Bidirectional BFS on every shortest-path problem—or only when you can clearly bound the graph and have a good meeting strategy?
